newsitem.title: USA: RAYTHEON $3 BLN DEBT DEAL SEES SUCCESSFUL LANDING.
newsitem.headline: RAYTHEON $3 BLN DEBT DEAL SEES SUCCESSFUL LANDING.

text.p: After a rousing launch, defense contractor Raytheon Co's $3.0 billion multi-tranche debt offering landed successfully on the corporate bond market, dealers said.
"The deal was a blowout. I'm hearing that every single tranche is currently issue-plus bid on the Street," said one high-grade syndicate source.
Initially slated to come as a $2.5 billion three-part debt offering, the deal was boosted in size to meet strong demand by investors, dealers said.
"It went extremely well ... some accounts were only able to get 10 percent allocation, there was so much demand out there," another player said.
John Huber, portfolio manager for Galliard Capital Management, said Raytheon's debt offering would be "a core holding" for a lot of portfolio managers.

"It's a new name," Huber said. "Raytheon has only two other debt issues outstanding, so you're looking at a limited amount of supply and it's a higher quality industrial company that has stable operating earnings."
Raytheon's multi-tranche debt offering included the following tranches, dealers said.
-- $500 million in three-year notes, at 34 basis points
over U.S. Treasuries,
-- $1.0 billion five-year notes, at 41 basis points
-- $1.0 billion 10-year notes at 61 basis points over
-- $500 million in 30-year debt at 75 basis points over
Morgan Stanley Dean Witter, Bear Stearns & Co and Credit Suisse First Boston were joint lead underwriters for the deal.
"We were very pleased with the offering -- it far exceeded our expectations," said Robert McWade, a spokesman for Raytheon Co.
"Investor interest was quite high and we think this is an endorsement of our strategy and where the company is headed," McWade said.
McWade said proceeds from the offfering will be used by Raytheon to finance its $2.95 billion acquisition of Texas Instruments Inc's defense and electronics unit.
Michael Gray, an investment officer at Massachusetts Financial Services Inc said the company's strategy for moving ahead has worked well.

Gray said the firm's defense operations have done well and seems to be pretty comfortable with its financial strategy while continuing to target significant credit improvement over the intermediate term.
"They're going to be real leveraged with defense electronics, which is kind of where you want to be in terms of the profitability perspective," Gray said.
"That being said, the businesses that they're going to own ... the defense segments that they're going to operate are very high margin, high quality value-added segments, Gray said.

"In the realm of the consolidation that's occurred within the industry, they needed to do something; so they were aggressive and they paid the price on ratings, but the firm's planning to get back to a AAA rating," Gray said.
Currently, Raytheon's senior debt is rated BBB by Standard & Poor's and Baa1 by Moody's Investors Service.

Gray said one major factor going forward would be Raytheon's near-term reemergence in the market to fund its pending acquisition of Hughes Electronics Corp's defense operations for $9.5 billion in debt and equity.
"We'd like to know what kind of dislocation effect, if any, that additional supply is going to have," Gray said.

Richard Swift, managing director at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said, "Maximum debt for both Hughes and Texas Instrument transactions were slated for $4.5 billion and that's with an adverse movement in the collar."
The Hughes Electronics unit purchase will include $5.1 bln in equity financing with the remainder in debt.

"There was a collar and right now Raytheon stock is in excess of the collar, which means if things do not change than the equity value of the deal will go from $5.1 billion to $5.6 billion," said Swift. "The firm would have a commensurate reduction in the amount of debt they'll need."

"If the stock range goes to the low part of the collar they'll come back and issue $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion in debt; but obviously, at the high end of the collar, that number gets reduced," Swift added.

The $500 million three-year tranche that was added on to the current transaction should help reduce the amount of any future issue, Swift said. Noting that $3.0 billion in debt has already been issued, Swift predicted the next offering would probably come at between 1.0 to $1.5 billion.
"They've (Raytheon) have been pretty clear with the marketplace in terms of different maturities ... they won't throw out bonds of a similar nature on top of this one," Swift said.
"Bondbuyers like to know that they're not going to get hit with the same paper and have it impact the price of what they've just purchased," he added.
Swift noted that the current $3.0 billion debt offering "was oversubscribed in all tranches with the 30-year meeting the strongest demand."
When asked why the 30-year tranche was not increased in size, Swift said:
"From a corporate finance standpoint this company doesn't need or want more long money than $500 million in 30-years."

"When they consolidate the defense operations of Texas Instruments and Hughes Electronics, this company will be a tremendous cash flow generator and this cash will allow them to pay down debt fairly quickly. That being the case they don't want to get stuck with a lot of long 30-year paper."
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, U.S. corporate bond unit,
